walkthroughs.body_html:
Foundations of Physics — a core area of A-Level Physics.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Foundations of Physics brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Foundations of Physics.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

options: udd
uud
uds
uuu

mcqs.q: In β⁻ decay, the exchange particle is:
options: Photon
W⁻ boson
Gluon
Z boson

mcqs.q: Does light always travel at the same speed?
options: Only in a vacuum; in any material medium (water, glass) light travels more slowly, which is what causes refraction.
No — light always slows with distance from its source.
The horizontal velocity increases over time because the projectile is falling.
Yes — c is a universal constant in every situation.

mcqs.q: For a projectile launched horizontally, what affects the horizontal component of velocity during flight (ignoring air resistance)?
options: No — light always slows with distance from its source.
Gravity slows down both the vertical and horizontal motion.
The horizontal velocity increases over time because the projectile is falling.
Nothing — horizontal velocity stays constant; only vertical velocity changes due to gravity.

mcqs.q: How does the maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons depend on light intensity?
options: The horizontal velocity increases over time because the projectile is falling.
Higher intensity gives photoelectrons more kinetic energy.
Intensity has no effect on anything in the photoelectric effect.
It does not — max KE depends only on the frequency of the light; intensity affects the rate (number) of electrons emitted.
